idea: Replace the random order with a target-similarity filter. (1) Fit a TfidfVectorizer on character n-grams (analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(1,3), sublinear_tf=True, max_features about 50k) using the first 2000 characters of each doc; train a LogisticRegression (C=1, class_weight='balanced') with the 200 target_sample docs as positives and a seeded random sample of 3000 pool docs as negatives; score every pool doc with predict_proba. (2) Drop exact and near duplicates: keep only the first doc per hash of its whitespace-normalised, lower-cased first 500 characters. (3) Drop junk: docs shorter than 200 characters, or with a unique-word ratio below 0.2, or with less than 80% alphabetic/space characters. (4) Count tokens with tiktoken gpt2 (encode_ordinary_batch; fall back to len(text)/4 if time is short). Sort the surviving docs by score descending and take docs from the top until the cumulative token count reaches T; if the docs with score > 0.5 hold fewer than T tokens, still fill up to T with the next best scored docs rather than cycling. (5) Shuffle the selected indices with random.Random(int(os.environ.get('CURATE_SEED', 0))) and return them.
why: The pool is about half spam, forum, Q&A and news text while the target is WikiText-style Wikipedia articles (" = Title = ", " @-@ " tokenisation), so spending all T tokens on deduplicated, target-like documents should cut bpb far more than a random half of the noisy pool.
outcome: dev 1.9462 against 1.9590 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Stop padding the selection with off-domain documents; train only on the confidently target-like set and repeat it. Keep the dedup, junk filter and classifier unchanged. After scoring, define the high-confidence set H as survivors with predict_proba >= 0.5. Count the tokens of H with tiktoken. If H holds at least T tokens, behave as now (take top-scored docs until T, then a seeded shuffle). If H holds fewer than T tokens, do NOT fill with lower-scored docs. Instead, take all of H (if H is under 0.2*T tokens, extend it with the next best scored docs until it reaches 0.2*T, to avoid extreme repetition). Build the returned list as consecutive epochs of H, each epoch a fresh shuffle from the CURATE_SEED-seeded RNG, appended until the cumulative token count reaches T. The result is that every training token comes from target-like text, with each doc seen about T/tokens(H) times. Have the implementer report tokens(H)/T and the number of docs in H, so the next experiment can use those figures.
why: The first filter only gained 0.013 bpb, which suggests the pool has well under T tokens of target-like (WikiText-style) text and the top-T fill is diluting it with spam, code and web text; a few repeats of in-domain text over 300 steps should beat that off-domain filler.
outcome: dev 1.9399 against 1.9462 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a damaged-text filter on top of the current best, leaving everything else unchanged (dedup, junk filter, classifier, top-score fill to T, seeded shuffle). The pool contains wiki-style articles with character-level corruption (e.g. 'Brazilian reams', 'jzz', 'Augst') and mojibake ('â€™', 'Â'), which the char n-gram classifier still scores as target-like.

1. Build a vocabulary V from the pool: lower-case each doc's first 3000 chars, extract words with the regex [a-z]+, and count document frequency. V is the set of words with document frequency >= 5, plus every word that occurs in target_sample.
2. For each doc compute oov = the fraction of its words of length >= 4 (first 3000 chars) that are not in V. For target_sample docs, compute the same rate against the pool-only vocabulary (without adding target words), so the threshold is not biased. Set thr = max(1.5 * the 95th percentile of the target rates, 0.02).
3. Drop survivors with oov > thr.
4. Drop survivors whose first 3000 chars have more than 1 occurrence per 1000 chars of the mojibake markers 'â€', 'Ã', 'Â' or '�'.
5. Apply both filters before the classifier ranking; then fill to T from the top-scored remaining docs as now.

Have the implementer report how many docs and tokens each filter removes, and the tokens (as a fraction of T) of remaining docs with score >= 0.5.
why: Typo-corrupted copies of target-like articles pass the current filters and teach the model wrong spellings, so removing them should free budget for clean text and lower bpb; separately, experiment 2 is logged as rejected although its dev bpb (1.9399) is lower than the best (1.9462), which is worth checking.
outcome: dev 1.9420 against 1.9462 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a word-order (shuffled-text) filter on top of the current best; leave dedup, junk filter, classifier, top-score fill to T and the seeded shuffle unchanged. The pool contains wiki-style articles whose words are shuffled within sentences (e.g. 'Simpsons fourteenth of fifth " " episode ' vs. Lisa the is season'). A char n-gram classifier cannot see this, so it ranks them as target-like.

1. Tokenise by lower-casing and whitespace split (the target is already space-tokenised), using the first 3000 chars of each doc.
2. Build B = the set of adjacent word bigrams that occur at least 2 times across all 200 target_sample docs (full text).
3. For a doc, define rate = the fraction of its adjacent word pairs that are in B.
4. Calibrate the threshold by cross-fitting: split target_sample into two halves, build the bigram set from each half (count >= 2) and compute the rate for the docs of the other half. Set thr = 0.7 * the 5th percentile of these 200 held-out rates.
5. Drop survivors with rate < thr before the classifier ranking. Pool docs are scored against the full-sample B, so the half-sample threshold is conservative for intact text.
6. Then fill to T from the top-scored remaining docs as now.

Have the implementer report: the target held-out rate distribution (5th, 50th and 95th percentile), the pool rate histogram, the number of docs and tokens removed, how many removed docs had classifier score >= 0.5, and the tokens (as a fraction of T) of remaining docs with score >= 0.5.
why: Word-shuffled wiki articles pass the char n-gram classifier yet teach wrong word order, so removing them with a target-bigram hit rate should replace damaged text with intact text in the T-token budget.
outcome: dev 1.9172 against 1.9462 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Change only the final ordering; keep dedup, junk filter, word-order filter, classifier and the top-score fill to T exactly as they are. After the fill, split the selected docs into two blocks by classifier score: H = selected docs with score >= 0.5 and L = selected docs with score < 0.5 (the filler). Shuffle each block separately with the CURATE_SEED-seeded RNG and return L followed by H, so the off-domain filler is read first and the target-like text is read in the final steps of training. Do not repeat any docs and do not change which docs are selected. If L is empty or H is empty, fall back to the current single seeded shuffle. If the classifier failed (scores is None), keep the current behaviour. Have the implementer report the docs and tokens (as a fraction of T) in H and in L, so the next experiment knows how much of the budget is filler. Note for the reviewer: experiments 2 and 3 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb (1.9399 and 1.9420) was lower than the best at the time (1.9462); I cannot explain that from the log and have avoided both ideas as instructed.
why: With only 300 steps, the model should end up closest to the text it sees last, so reading the low-score filler first and the target-like docs last should lower target bpb without changing the selected set.
outcome: dev 1.9172 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a tokens-per-character damage demotion to the current best. Keep dedup, junk filter, word-order filter, classifier and the final seeded shuffle unchanged; change only the order in which docs are taken during the fill.

1. Tokenise all survivors of the word-order filter up front with tiktoken gpt2 (encode_ordinary_batch, 8 threads, batches of about 512, full text). Store exact token counts and reuse them in the fill, so nothing is tokenised twice. If the time guard trips, fall back to the current behaviour for the docs not yet tokenised and treat them as not damaged.
2. For each doc compute tpc = tokens / characters. Compute the same for the 200 target_sample docs.
3. Set thr = the 97.5th percentile of the target tpc values. Character-corrupted words ('Augst', 'jzz') and mojibake ('â€™', 'Â') split into more BPE tokens, so damaged articles have a higher tpc than clean ones.
4. Mark a survivor as 'damaged' if tpc > thr. Do not drop it; demote it.
5. Fill order: first the non-damaged docs with score >= 0.5, by score descending; then the damaged docs with score >= 0.5, by score descending; then all remaining docs, by score descending. Take docs until T tokens, as now.
6. Apply the single seeded shuffle to the selection, as now.

Have the implementer report: the target tpc percentiles (5th, 50th, 97.5th) and thr; a histogram of tpc over survivors with score >= 0.5; the docs and tokens (as a fraction of T) in each of the three tiers; and how many tokens of each tier ended up in the selection.

Note for the reviewer: this targets the same damaged text as rejected experiment 3, but with a different signal (BPE tokens per character rather than out-of-vocabulary rate and mojibake markers) and by demoting rather than dropping. Experiment 5 scored exactly the same as the best (1.9172), which suggests its filler block was empty and that docs with score >= 0.5 already hold at least T tokens; I have not confirmed this from a log, and the tier report in this experiment will show it.
why: If target-like docs already exceed the budget, the gain left is in choosing the clean ones, and tokens per character is a cheap damage signal that also favours docs giving more training bytes per token.
outcome: dev 1.9095 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a title-level dedup on top of the current best, leaving the junk filter, word-order filter, classifier, top-score fill to T and the seeded shuffle unchanged. The pool appears to hold several versions of the same wiki article (clean, word-shuffled, character-corrupted), and the current dedup only catches copies whose first 500 characters are identical.

1. For every doc that survives the word-order filter, take the first line (text up to the first '\n', stripped). If it matches the heading pattern '^= [^=].* =$' and is at most 200 chars, use its lower-cased, whitespace-normalised form as the title key. Docs without such a heading get no key and are never grouped.
2. Group survivors by title key. In each group with more than one doc, keep exactly one: the doc with the highest word-order rate (already computed against the full-sample bigram set B). Break ties by the longer doc, then by the lower index. Drop the others.
3. Run this after the word-order filter and before the classifier ranking, so the freed budget is filled by the next best scored distinct articles.
4. If the word-order filter was skipped (no rates), keep the longest doc per group instead.

Have the implementer report: the number of title groups with more than one doc, the docs and estimated tokens (as a fraction of T) removed, the distribution of group sizes, and the tokens (as a fraction of T) of remaining docs with score >= 0.5, so we know whether the fill now reaches into off-domain filler.

Note for the reviewer: experiments 2, 3 and 6 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb (1.9399, 1.9420, 1.9095) was lower than the best at the time. I cannot explain that from the log, so I have not built on them. This is a different mechanism (removing repeated articles, not detecting damage). I have not confirmed from a log that same-title variants survive the current filters; the group report will show it.
why: If clean and damaged copies of the same article both survive, the budget is spent on repeated content, and keeping only the most intact copy per title should swap that for more distinct target-like text.
outcome: dev 1.9278 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a pool-consensus fluency ranking to the fill, on top of the current best. Keep dedup, junk filter, word-order filter, classifier and the final seeded shuffle unchanged; change only the order in which docs are taken during the fill.

1. After scoring, let H = survivors with classifier score >= 0.5.
2. Build a bigram document-frequency table from H plus target_sample. Lower-case and whitespace-split the first 6000 chars of each doc, and count each adjacent word bigram once per doc. Let B2 = bigrams with document frequency >= 3. Target_sample docs count towards the frequency.
3. For each doc in H compute flu = (number of its adjacent word pairs in the first 6000 chars that are in B2) / (number of pairs). A doc's own contribution is at most 1 of the 3 required, so damaged or idiosyncratic bigrams do not qualify themselves.
4. Calibrate on the target: compute flu for the 200 target_sample docs against the same B2, and set thr = the 10th percentile of the target values.
5. Fill order:
   - Tier A: docs in H with flu >= thr, by classifier score descending.
   - Tier B: docs in H with flu < thr, by flu descending.
   - Tier C: all remaining survivors, by classifier score descending.
   Take docs until T tokens, as now. Nothing is dropped; low-fluency docs are only used if the budget needs them.
6. Apply the single seeded shuffle to the selection, as now.
7. Time guard: if step 2 or 3 would pass 125 s since the start, skip the tiering and use the current order.

Have the implementer report: the target flu percentiles (10th, 50th, 90th) and thr; a histogram of flu over H; the docs and tokens (as a fraction of T) in tiers A, B and C; and how many tokens of each tier ended up in the selection.

Note for the reviewer: experiments 2, 3 and 6 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb (1.9399, 1.9420, 1.9095) was lower than the best at the time. I cannot explain that from the log, so I have not repeated them. This overlaps in aim with experiments 3 and 6 (it would also demote damaged text), but the signal is different: word-bigram support across the pool's own target-like docs, rather than out-of-vocabulary rate, mojibake markers or tokens per character. I have not confirmed from a log that partially shuffled or corrupted articles survive the current filters; the tier report will show it.
why: Wiki-like docs that are partially shuffled or character-corrupted probably still pass the conservative word-order threshold and the char n-gram classifier, and ranking by pool-wide bigram support should fill the budget with clean target-like text first.
outcome: dev 1.9094 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Tighten the word-order filter's threshold calibration; leave dedup, junk filter, classifier, top-score fill to T and the seeded shuffle unchanged.

The current threshold is loose in two ways. It is calibrated on half-sample bigram sets (100 docs), while pool docs are scored against the full-sample set (200 docs), which gives them higher rates. It is then multiplied by 0.7. Lightly or partially shuffled articles may therefore pass.

1. Replace the two-half cross-fit with a 10-fold cross-fit. Split target_sample into 10 folds using the existing seed + 7919 stream. For each fold, build the bigram set (count >= 2, full text) from the other 9 folds and compute the rate of the held-out docs on their first 3000 chars. This matches the roughly 200-doc set that pool docs are scored against.
2. Set thr = the 2nd percentile of the 200 held-out rates, with no 0.7 factor (ORDER_FACTOR = 1.0, ORDER_PCT = 2.0).
3. Score pool docs against the full-sample bigram set as now and drop survivors with rate < thr.
4. Keep the existing safeguards: skip the filter if fewer than 20 held-out rates are usable or if it would remove everything.
5. Add one safeguard: if the remaining docs with classifier score >= 0.5 hold fewer than T tokens, log this clearly. Still fill from the next best scored docs as now.

Have the implementer report: the old threshold (0.7 * 5th percentile of the two-half rates) and the new threshold; the target held-out percentiles (2nd, 5th, 50th); the pool rate histogram; the docs and estimated tokens (as a fraction of T) removed in total; the docs and tokens removed that the old threshold would have kept, and how many of those had classifier score >= 0.5; and the tokens (as a fraction of T) of remaining docs with score >= 0.5.

Note for the reviewer: experiments 2, 3, 6 and 8 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb (1.9399, 1.9420, 1.9095, 1.9094) was lower than the best at the time. I cannot explain that from the log, so I have not repeated or built on them. This experiment only recalibrates the one filter that was kept (experiment 4). I have not confirmed from a log that shuffled docs survive the current threshold; the report on newly removed docs will show it.
why: The kept word-order filter gave the largest gain so far (1.9462 to 1.9172), but its threshold is doubly loose, so tightening it should remove shuffled articles that still take up budget.
outcome: dev 1.8349 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Tighten the word-order filter again, the only change that has been kept twice, and make it cover the whole document. Leave dedup, junk filter, classifier, top-score fill to T and the seeded shuffle unchanged.

1. Compute the word-order rate over the full text of each doc instead of the first 3000 chars (ORDER_WINDOW = None), for pool docs and for the held-out target docs in the 10-fold cross-fit. The bigram set B stays as now (count >= 2 over the full text of target_sample). Time guard: if the pool rate pass would run beyond 45 s since the start, use the first 12000 chars for the remaining docs, and calibrate the target on the same window.

2. Choose the threshold adaptively from the held-out target rates, with candidates at the 10th, 5th and 2nd percentile (no factor). Compute rates for all dedup+junk survivors first, then score all of them with the classifier (move the scoring ahead of the drop), and tokenise or estimate their tokens. Pick the strictest candidate (10th, then 5th, then 2nd) for which the docs with rate >= thr and classifier score >= 0.5 still hold at least 1.05 T tokens. If none qualifies, use the 2nd percentile as now.

3. Drop survivors with rate < the chosen thr, then fill to T from the top-scored remaining docs as now.

4. Keep the existing safeguards: skip the filter if fewer than 20 held-out rates are usable or if it would remove everything.

Have the implementer report: the target held-out percentiles (2nd, 5th, 10th, 50th) on the full text; the pool rate histogram; for each candidate threshold, the docs and tokens (as a fraction of T) removed and the tokens of remaining docs with score >= 0.5; which candidate was chosen; and how many docs kept by the current rule (first 3000 chars, 2nd percentile) are now removed.

Note for the reviewer: experiments 2, 3, 6 and 8 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb was lower than the best at the time. I cannot explain that from the log, so I have not repeated or built on them. I have not confirmed from a log that partly shuffled docs survive the current threshold; the per-candidate report will show it.
why: Tightening the word-order threshold gave the largest gain so far (1.9172 to 1.8349), which suggests partly shuffled articles still pass; a stricter, full-document threshold that never pushes the fill into off-domain filler should remove more of them.
outcome: dev 1.8354 against 1.8349 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Add a second-stage "clean target vs. surviving candidates" discriminator on top of the current best. Leave dedup, junk filter, word-order filter (10-fold, 2nd percentile, first 3000 chars), first-stage classifier and the final seeded shuffle unchanged.

The first-stage classifier separates the target from a random pool sample, so it only learns "wiki-like vs. other domains". The second stage is trained after the filters, so its negatives are the docs that still compete for the budget, and it can learn whatever still separates them from clean target text.

1. After first-stage scoring, let H = survivors with score >= 0.5. Skip the whole stage (use current behaviour) if H has fewer than 500 docs, if the first-stage classifier failed, or if more than 105 s have passed since the start. To make room, lower FEATURE_DEADLINE to 80 s and drop the report-only scoring of removed docs.
2. Training set: positives = the 200 target_sample docs; negatives = a seeded random sample of min(3000, |H|) docs from H. Use the first 1500 chars of each. Features: TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(2,5), sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2, max_features=200000, dtype=float32), fitted on this training set. Model: LogisticRegression(C=0.5, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=1000, random_state=seed).
3. Calibrate by 5-fold cross-fit, with folds drawn from a seed + 104729 stream over positives and negatives. For each fold, fit on the other four and record decision_function for the held-out target docs. Set thr2 = the 5th percentile of the 200 held-out target values.
4. Fit the final model on the whole training set and score all of H (first 1500 chars; shrink the prefix if needed to finish by 140 s). Negatives used in training are scored by the final model like the rest.
5. Mark docs in H with decision value < thr2 as "off-target". Fill order: non-flagged H docs by first-stage score descending; then flagged H docs by second-stage value descending; then the remaining survivors by first-stage score descending. Take docs until T tokens, as now. Flagged docs are therefore only used if the clean ones hold fewer than T tokens.
6. Apply the single seeded shuffle to the selection, as now.

Have the implementer report: the held-out target decision percentiles (5th, 50th, 95th) and thr2; a histogram of the second-stage values over H; docs and tokens (as a fraction of T) flagged; tokens of each tier that ended up in the selection; the first 150 chars of 10 flagged docs (lowest values) so we can see what is being caught; and total time.

Note for the reviewer: experiments 2, 3, 6 and 8 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb (1.9399, 1.9420, 1.9095, 1.9094) was lower than the best at the time. I cannot explain that from the log, so I have not repeated them. This overlaps in aim with experiments 3, 6 and 8 (it may also demote damaged text), but the mechanism is different: a learned discriminator against the surviving candidates, not a hand-made damage signal. I have not confirmed from a log that damaged or off-style docs remain in H; the flagged-doc report will show it.
why: Experiment 5 scoring exactly the same as the best suggests wiki-like docs already fill the budget, so the remaining gain should come from choosing the cleanest docs within that set, which a discriminator trained against the surviving candidates and calibrated on held-out target scores can learn without a hand-made rule.
outcome: dev 1.8192 against 1.8349 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Change only the fill order inside H, so the second-stage discriminator (the last kept change) decides which H docs are taken, not just which are flagged. Leave dedup, junk filter, word-order filter, both classifiers, thr2 and the final seeded shuffle unchanged.

1. Out-of-fold values for the training negatives. The 5-fold cross-fit already fits one model per fold. In each fold, also record decision_function for the held-out negatives (currently only the held-out target docs are recorded). After the final model has scored all of H, replace the value of each training negative with its out-of-fold value. This removes the in-sample bias that pushes the ~3000 training negatives below the other H docs. If a negative has no out-of-fold value (fold skipped), keep its final-model value.

2. New fill order. Rank all of H by second-stage value descending (out-of-fold for training negatives, final model for the rest). Then append the remaining survivors (first-stage score < 0.5) by first-stage score descending. Take docs until T tokens, as now. This amounts to using the strictest second-stage threshold that still fills the budget, instead of the fixed 5th-percentile flag with first-stage order above it.

3. Fallbacks stay as they are: if the second stage is skipped or abandoned, use first-stage score order.

4. Time: no new model fits. The only added work is decision_function on the held-out negatives in each fold. Keep all existing deadlines.

Have the implementer report: the second-stage value of the last H doc taken (the effective cut) and which percentile of the held-out target values it corresponds to; tokens (as a fraction of T) in H and in H above thr2; how many selected docs differ from the selection the current rule would have made (docs and tokens); mean in-sample vs out-of-fold value of the training negatives; and the first 150 chars of 10 H docs just below the effective cut.

Note for the reviewer: I have not confirmed from a log that non-flagged H holds more than T tokens. If it holds less, the selection is the same as now and dev bpb should be unchanged. Experiments 2, 3, 6 and 8 are logged as rejected although their dev bpb was lower than the best at the time; I cannot explain that from the log and have not repeated them.
why: The first-stage score only separates wiki-like text from other domains and is probably saturated within H, so ranking H by the second-stage value (which gave the latest gain) should fill the budget with the candidates closest to clean target text.
outcome: dev 1.8349 against 1.8192 for the best at the time, rejected
